big_idea: Dice rolls are POSSIBLE 1-6. We predict the MODE after many rolls.
learning_intention: We are learning to predict the mode of dice rolls.
student_learning_goal: I can predict the mode of dice rolls.
success_criteria: I can find the MODE of many rolls.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Lucky and Mae — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.

minds_on.hook: Mae: I'll roll this die 10 times. Predict the MODE — the most common number! Mae opens: 'Each roll is FRESH — the die FORGETS!'
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Lucky and Mae puppets. 'Friends — yesterday spinners. Today DICE and MODE.'

Review vocabulary. 'Mode = most common result. Dice rolls are POSSIBLE 1-6 — all equally likely.'

Demo. Roll a die. 'Got 4. Tally |.' Roll again. 'Got 2. Tally.' Roll 8 more times. Record on a tally chart.

Example tally:
1: |||
2: ||
3: |
4: |||
5: |
6: ||

'Total: 12 rolls (across 6 numbers, expecting roughly 2 each but RANDOM).'

Find mode. '4 has 3 (highest!). Mode = 4.'

More demos. Different rolls. Sometimes mode is 5, sometimes 1.

'Mae says — even though all 6 are EQUALLY POSSIBLE, after rolling MANY times, ONE number usually appears most. That's the MODE.'

Introduce D2.2 idea. 'If we roll AGAIN — same die — does the same number become mode? Maybe. Maybe not. Each TRIAL is a fresh test.'

'Today YOU roll and find modes.'

steps.instruction: Whole group: roll die 12 times. Find the mode.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say: 'Tally each roll. Mode = highest tally.'

steps.instruction: Three stations. A: Roll 12 times, find mode. B: Roll 20 times, find mode. C: Compare modes from 2 different rolls.
Stretch at C: predict if same mode will appear in a 3rd roll.
Discuss randomness. 'Every roll is a fresh test. Mode can change.'

STRATEGY COMPARE: After Station A, two pairs share HOW they could PREDICT mode of 6 rolls. Pair A 'guess my favourite'; Pair B 'roll-and-record-then-predict'; Pair C 'each face has 1/6 chance.' Class debates which is most reliable. Cite Konold (1989) — outcome-orientation gives way to long-run frequency thinking.
steps.teacher_prompt: Mae: 'Predicting a SINGLE roll is a guess. Predicting MANY rolls uses the math.'

differentiation.for_movement_learners: Roll with whole-body action; tally on a giant floor chart. NO-PAPER VERSION: finger-dice — child holds up 1-6 fingers behind their back, partner says STOP, child reveals; treat as fair die. Body becomes the die.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: rolls; records; finds mode.

discussion_prompts: Mae's preview: tomorrow we test mode across MANY trials (Lesson 5 — D2.2 bridge). What did today teach about predicting mode after just 6 rolls?
consolidation.exit_routine: Mae's fresh-die refrain — Mae calls 'Each roll is FRESH —' Class: 'the die FORGETS!' (3x with open-palm wipe). Each child writes one prediction on a sticky.

assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Lesson 4 captures D2.2 mastery for mode in dice rolls.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child predicts SAME MODE will repeat — repairing the same-mode-always trap at Grade 2
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On dice predictions, the trap is the gambler's-fallacy / representativeness heuristic (Kahneman & Tversky 1972; Fischbein 1975 primary intuitions; Konold 1989 outcome approach): child thinks 'rolled 6 last time, won't roll 6 again' OR 'always rolls my favourite number'. The fix: each roll is independent, the die has no memory.

Yesterday Lesson 3 used proportional reasoning on spinners. Today extends to fair dice. Lesson 5 capstones with mode prediction across populations (D2.2 bridge).
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair at C. First roll mode = 4. Child says next roll's mode WILL also be 4.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch. 'Your first roll mode was 4. But Mae asks — was it because 4 is special? Or just chance?'

Guide. 'Each roll is FRESH. The die has no memory. Next time, mode could be 1, 2, 3, 5, or 6.'

Roll second time. Show different mode.

Generlise. 'Lucky says — predict mode for ONE TRIAL. Different trials = often different modes. That's RANDOM.'

If still predicting same: provide a journal of multiple trials' modes. 'See — they vary.'
common_misconceptions: Same mode every time. (Repair: random — varies.)
Mode = die's preferred number. (Repair: dice have no preference.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child says 'won't roll 6 again': demo 10 rolls in a row; child sees that 6 can repeat. Drill 'fresh die, fresh roll.'
DIAGNOSTIC B — child predicts favourite number always: cover the die with a cup, child predicts; reveal; child sees prediction doesn't change reality.
DIAGNOSTIC C — child knows uniform distribution but can't predict mode of 6 rolls: drill 'over MANY rolls each face appears about EQUALLY — for 6 rolls, mode might be ANY face.'

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice of D2.2 dice mode.

parts_outline.task: Roll a die 12 times. Tally results. Find mode.
Roll AGAIN 12 times. Find mode. Compare to first roll.
Predict the mode of a 3rd roll. Test it.
